\section[dēspērō, dēspērāre]{dēspērō, dēspērāre — to despair (of)}

\label{lesson:LA-C498-despero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for annoyance, then the Latin for to torment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēspērō, dēspērāre}
\textbf{dēspērō, dēspērāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to despair (of)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Medicus dē salūte aegrī dēspērat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The doctor despairs of the patient's recovery.}
\end{quote}

\emph{dēspērō, dēspērāre, dēspērāvī, dēspērātum}: \emph{dē-} 'away from' + \emph{spērō} 'to hope'. With \emph{dē} and the ablative, or the accusative. English \emph{despair}, \emph{desperate}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dēspērō} is built on \emph{dē-} \textquotedblleft{}away from\textquotedblright{} and \emph{spērō} \textquotedblleft{}to hope\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{spēs} \textquotedblleft{}hope\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short). English \emph{despair} and \emph{desperate} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dēspērō, dēspērāre}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dēspērō, dēspērāre}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{dēspērō, dēspērāre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for annoyance, then the Latin for to torment, then say \emph{dēspērō, dēspērāre} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dēspērātiō, dēspērātiōnis]{dēspērātiō, dēspērātiōnis — despair, hopelessness}

\label{lesson:LA-C498-desperatio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to torment, then the Latin for to despair.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēspērātiō, dēspērātiōnis}
\textbf{dēspērātiō, dēspērātiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}despair, hopelessness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
In dēspērātiōne nautae deōs ōrant.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In their despair the sailors pray to the gods.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, third declension. English \emph{desperation}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dēspērātiō} is the action noun of \emph{dēspērō} \textquotedblleft{}to despair\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short). English \emph{desperation} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[cōnfīdō, cōnfīdere]{cōnfīdō, cōnfīdere — to trust, rely on; to be confident}

\label{lesson:LA-C498-confido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to despair, then the Latin for despair.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōnfīdō, cōnfīdere}
\textbf{cōnfīdō, cōnfīdere} — \textquotedblleft{}to trust, rely on; to be confident\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Amīcō meō omnīnō cōnfīdō.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I trust my friend completely.}
\end{quote}

Semi-deponent: \emph{cōnfīdō, cōnfīdere, cōnfīsus sum}, with the dative of a person. English \emph{confide}, \emph{confident}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cōnfīdō} is built on \emph{con-} and \emph{fīdō} \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); EtymDB traces \emph{fīdō} through Proto-Italic to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{confide} and \emph{confident} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[diffīdō, diffīdere]{diffīdō, diffīdere — to distrust; to lose hope}

\label{lesson:LA-C498-diffido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for despair, then the Latin for to trust.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: diffīdō, diffīdere}
\textbf{diffīdō, diffīdere} — \textquotedblleft{}to distrust; to lose hope\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mercātor nautīs diffīdit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The merchant distrusts the sailors.}
\end{quote}

Semi-deponent: \emph{diffīdō, diffīdere, diffīsus sum}, with the dative. The opposite of \emph{cōnfīdō}. English \emph{diffident}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{diffīdō} is built on \emph{dis-} \textquotedblleft{}apart, not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{fīdō} \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{diffident} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[crēdulus, crēdula, crēdulum]{crēdulus, crēdula, crēdulum — trusting, credulous}

\label{lesson:LA-C498-credulus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to trust, then the Latin for to distrust.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: crēdulus, crēdula, crēdulum}
\textbf{crēdulus, crēdula, crēdulum} — \textquotedblleft{}trusting, credulous\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Puer crēdulus omnia crēdit, quae audit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The trusting boy believes everything he hears.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{crēdō} — to believe. English \emph{credulous}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{crēdulus} is built on \emph{crēdō} \textquotedblleft{}to believe\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-ulus} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB), and EtymDB traces \emph{crēdō} to a Proto-Indo-European phrase meaning \textquotedblleft{}to put one’s heart\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{credulous} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
